description: ChimneySaver Water Repellent tops 6 chimney sealers for most brick. Breathable picks for brick, dense masonry and cracked crowns, and what leaks first.
dek: ChimneySaver Water Repellent tops 6 chimney sealers for most brick.
intro: ChimneySaver Water Repellent is the best chimney sealer for most homes: a breathable siloxane repellent made for chimney brick that stops rain soaking in while letting moisture inside the masonry escape. For dense, hard-fired brick, Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 reaches deeper, and for a cracked crown you need a separate coating such as ChimneyRX.

Before you buy anything, know that brick is rarely the only leak. Cracked crowns, failed flashing and missing caps let in more water than porous brick does. A repellent is still one of the best things you can do for chimney masonry, because it slows the soaking that leads to spalled faces and crumbling joints, but it works best as one part of a short list of repairs.
quickAnswer: Spray a vapor-permeable siloxane or silane-siloxane repellent on the brick and mortar, brush an elastomeric crown coating on a sound crown, reseal small flashing gaps with a flashing-rated sealant, and fit a cap. Never use paint, tar or a gloss sealer on chimney brick: they trap moisture and speed up spalling. Hose-test the chimney first so you fix the part that is actually leaking.

blocks.p: The first four go on the brick and mortar sides. The last two go only on the crown, the cap of concrete or mortar on top of the chimney, because a brick repellent cannot bridge cracks in a horizontal surface. Most chimneys that leak need one from each group.

Whatever you pick, check that the label calls it breathable or vapor permeable and rates it for above-grade vertical masonry. That one word on the can matters more on a chimney than on any other brick surface, for reasons covered further down.

sections.h: The 6 Best Chimney Sealers in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: The order reflects how many chimneys each product suits, based on maker technical data, the surfaces and exposures each is rated for, published vapor-permeability claims, warranty terms and recurring feedback from owners and chimney sweeps. Brick repellents come first; the crown coatings are ranked after them because they solve a different problem.

ChimneySaver is made by Saver Systems, a company that has concentrated on chimney and masonry repellents for decades, and it is the product many chimney sweeps carry on the truck. It is a penetrating siloxane repellent built around one priority: letting chimney masonry give off water vapor freely while stopping liquid rain from soaking in. That balance matters on a chimney because it is exposed on all four sides, takes wind-driven rain and also carries moisture up from combustion and condensation inside. The maker offers more than one formulation, including a water-based version, and backs it with a warranty when applied as directed. It goes on by low-pressure sprayer from the top down and dries with no visible change to brick or mortar. The drawbacks are availability and cost: general hardware stores often do not stock it, and it costs more per gallon than general masonry repellents.

**Pros:** made specifically for chimney masonry, high vapor permeability, invisible once dry, long track record with sweeps, warranty when applied per directions. **Cons:** harder to find in stores, pricier per gallon than general repellents.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=ChimneySaver+Water+Repellent&tag=sktiger-20)

Siloxa-Tek 8500 blends silane, a very small molecule that soaks deep into dense masonry, with siloxane, which works nearer the surface of more porous material. On a chimney of hard-fired brick with softer mortar joints, that mix treats both. It cures to an invisible, breathable repellent with no sheen. Because it is a general masonry repellent, it is a good choice when you want to treat the chimney and the brick walls of the house in one project with one sprayer. Coverage depends on porosity, so treat a small test area first to work out how much you need. Keep it off roofing, glass and painted trim, and wipe overspray promptly. It needs dry weather before and after application, and it sits at the premium end of the shelf.
**Pros:** reaches deep into dense brick, vapor permeable after cure, natural look, also suits brick walls, block and concrete. **Cons:** premium price, needs a dry spell on both sides of the job.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ghostshield+Siloxa-Tek+8500&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Budget: DRYLOK Clear Masonry Water Repellent

blocks.p: DRYLOK is one of the most familiar masonry brands, and its clear repellent is among the easiest chimney-suitable treatments to pick up at a home center. It is made to soak into above-grade brick, block and stucco and leave a clear, natural finish. On a single chimney, it does a reasonable job of cutting water absorption into the brick, which is the main goal of any repellent. It is less specialized than ChimneySaver, and dedicated silane-siloxane blends generally claim longer service lives, so plan to hose-test the chimney every year or two and reapply when water stops beading. Read the label to confirm it describes the product as breathable before using it on a chimney, and apply it only to clean, dry brick in mild, dry weather.

**Pros:** sold at most home centers, clear natural finish, rated for above-grade brick, block and stucco, low cost for one chimney. **Cons:** not chimney-specific, may need reapplying sooner than premium repellents.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DRYLOK+Clear+Masonry+Water+Repellent&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Water-Based: Foundation Armor SX5000 WB

blocks.p: SX5000 WB is a water-based silane-siloxane penetrating sealer rated for brick, concrete, pavers and block. On a roof, the water carrier is a real advantage: low odor and soap-and-water cleanup make a precarious job a little easier, and overspray comes off shingles and flashing more easily than solvent products. Like the others, it leaves no visible film and lets the brick breathe. It is good value if you want to treat the chimney, a brick patio and a block wall from one purchase. Apply it with a pump sprayer, flooding the surface, and add a second coat wet on wet on soft or very porous brick where the label allows. It must stay dry through its cure, which the maker lists at around a day.

**Pros:** low odor, breathable silane-siloxane chemistry, rated for brick, block and concrete, good value per gallon. **Cons:** must stay dry during cure, not chimney-specific, so check the label for vertical masonry use.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Foundation+Armor+SX5000+WB&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Crown Coating: ChimneyRX Brushable Crown Repair

blocks.p: The crown is one of the most common chimney leak points, and brick repellents are not made to fix it. ChimneyRX Brushable Crown Repair is an elastomeric coating designed for that surface. It brushes on in a thick layer, bridges hairline cracks and stays flexible as the crown expands and shrinks with the seasons, which is why cracks patched with rigid mortar alone keep reopening. It suits a crown that is structurally sound but showing fine cracks or a weathered, porous surface. It will not save a crown that is crumbling, broken into pieces or built without an overhang; those need rebuilding. Clean the crown, let it dry, fill wider cracks with the patch product the maker recommends, then coat it per the label and keep it off the flue liner.

**Pros:** bridges hairline crown cracks, brush-on with no special tools, flexible film moves with temperature, seals the most common leak point. **Cons:** crown only, cannot fix a crumbling or badly broken crown.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=ChimneyRX+Brushable+Crown+Repair&tag=sktiger-20)

CrownSeal is Saver Systems' crown coating, designed to pair with ChimneySaver on the brick. It forms a flexible, water-resistant layer on top of the crown that bridges small cracks while being formulated to let vapor escape. Many sweeps use the two as a set: CrownSeal on the crown, ChimneySaver on the sides. Like every crown coating, it is for crowns that are still intact. Large cracks, loose pieces or a thin mortar wash with no overhang call for a rebuild, ideally a properly formed concrete crown with a drip edge that projects past the brick. Apply only to clean, dry surfaces, and do not coat the flue liner or the joint between liner and crown unless the instructions allow it.

**Pros:** made by a chimney-focused company, flexible and breathable, bridges small cracks, matches ChimneySaver for a two-part system. **Cons:** sold mainly through chimney pros and specialty sellers, no substitute for rebuilding a failed crown.

sections.h: What Is the Best Breathable Sealant for Spalling Chimney Brick?

blocks.p: For spalling chimney brick, use a penetrating siloxane or silane-siloxane water repellent that the label describes as vapor permeable, such as ChimneySaver or Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500, and only after the damaged brick and mortar have been repaired. Spalling is a moisture problem, so the sealer has to keep rain out without keeping water in.

Spalling is when the face of a brick pops off in flakes or chunks. It usually comes from freeze-thaw cycles: water soaks into the brick, freezes, expands and breaks the surface. Soft brick, eroded mortar, a cracked crown and a non-breathable coating all make it worse. Brick fragments on the roof or in the gutter are a classic sign.

blocks.h3: Repellent protects, it does not rebuild

blocks.p: A repellent cannot glue a broken face back on or refill an eroded joint. Walk every side of the chimney first and note bricks with broken faces, mortar joints recessed more than about a quarter inch and mortar that crumbles when scraped with a screwdriver. Those spots let water in faster than any sealer can keep it out.

Repointing means raking out failed mortar to a depth of roughly two to three times the joint width and packing in fresh mortar in layers. On older chimneys the new mortar should usually be softer and more lime-rich than modern mixes, because mortar harder than the brick pushes stress and moisture into the brick, which then spalls. Individually failed bricks can be cut out and replaced; where many above the roofline have failed, a partial rebuild from the roof up is often the better value.

New mortar has to cure before the repellent goes on, and mortar makers commonly suggest waiting several weeks. A sensible plan is masonry repairs in late spring or summer and the repellent in early fall, so the chimney enters winter repaired, cured and protected. For the chemistry behind the two repellent families, see [silane vs siloxane sealers](/silane-vs-siloxane-sealers/).

sections.h: Where Do Chimney Leaks Start, and How Do You Find Them?

blocks.p: Chimney leaks show up as stains on the ceiling or wall next to the chimney, water in the firebox, a rusty damper or white efflorescence on interior brick. The water usually comes in at one of five places, and more than one can be at fault.

ul: **The crown:** the top slab that should shed water off the chimney. Many are built from plain mortar with no overhang or drip edge, and they crack with temperature swings.

**The flashing:** the metal where the chimney passes through the roof. When counterflashing pulls out of the mortar joints or its sealant dries out, water runs down into the attic and can appear some distance from where it entered.
**The cap:** without one, rain falls straight down the flue.
**The brick and mortar:** porous brick and eroded joints soak up rain on all four sides.
**Condensation in the flue:** moisture from combustion, especially with high-efficiency appliances or a fireplace used now and then in cold weather.

blocks.p: From the ground, use binoculars to check for cracked or missing crown pieces, a damaged or missing cap, bent or loose flashing, dark wet patches, white staining and spalled faces. Then go into the attic during or just after a rain to see where water appears.

With a helper inside watching, run a garden hose gently over one part of the chimney at a time for 10 to 15 minutes. Start low at the flashing, then move up to the brick, then the crown, then the cap. When water appears inside, you have found the entry point. Stop as soon as you see water so you do not soak the ceiling.

The National Fire Protection Association standard NFPA 211 calls for chimneys, fireplaces and vents to be inspected every year. A sweep certified by the Chimney Safety Institute of America can do a Level 1 or Level 2 inspection, including a camera scan of the flue, and will catch cracked liners or creosote buildup that no exterior sealer fixes. Deal with those safety problems first, then the water.

sections.h: Why Must a Chimney Sealer Breathe?

blocks.p: A chimney is always moving moisture. Rain soaks in from outside, and combustion and condensation add water from inside. The brick has to release that moisture through its outer face. If a coating blocks it, water builds up in the masonry, freezes, and breaks the brick apart from within.

Siloxane and silane-siloxane repellents soak into the pores of brick and mortar and line them with a water-repellent layer without filling them. Rain beads and runs off, but vapor still gets out. Film-forming products, including many paints, gloss acrylic sealers and roofing tar, sit on the surface and seal the water in. On a chimney, that speeds up exactly the damage you are trying to prevent.

blocks.h3: Will painting a leaking chimney breast in the loft help?

blocks.p: No. Painting the inside face of a damp chimney breast in an attic or loft only hides the stain for a while, and a non-breathable paint can trap moisture in the masonry. Find where the water enters outside, usually the crown, flashing or cap, and fix that. If the breast is damp from condensation inside an unused flue, ventilating the flue or capping it with a vented cap is the usual fix.

blocks.h3: Does a concrete sealer work on brick?

blocks.p: Only if it is a penetrating, breathable repellent rated for vertical masonry. Many silane-siloxane products sold for concrete are also rated for brick; film-forming acrylic concrete sealers are not suitable. The [best concrete sealer](/best-concrete-sealer/) guide explains which is which, and the [best brick sealer](/best-brick-sealer-reviews/) guide covers products for brick walls that overlap with chimney use.

sections.h: What Is the Best Sealer for a Chimney Crown or Cap?

blocks.p: For a crown with hairline cracks on an otherwise solid slab, an elastomeric crown coating such as ChimneyRX Brushable Crown Repair or ChimneySaver CrownSeal is the best fix. For a crown that is crumbling or built without an overhang, no coating will last; it needs rebuilding.

Inspect the crown up close only if you can reach it safely. Clear off moss, debris and loose material. Fill wider cracks with the patch compound the coating maker specifies, let everything dry, then brush on the coating at the thickness the label lists. Carry it to the edges so water cannot creep under it, and keep it off the flue liner unless the instructions allow it.

A crown that is broken into pieces, crumbling or poured as a thin mortar wash needs a rebuild. A proper crown is cast concrete, sloped to shed water, overhangs the brick by a couple of inches with a drip edge underneath so water falls clear, and has a bond break around the flue liner so the liner can expand on its own. This is mason or chimney contractor work. It costs more than a coating, but a well-built crown can last decades, while patching a failed one buys a season or two.

A chimney cap keeps rain, snow, birds and animals out of the flue. Stainless steel caps with a mesh screen also act as spark arrestors. Measure the flue tile or ask the sweep to fit one during an inspection. If a cap leaks where it meets the crown, reseal that joint with a sealant the cap maker recommends for masonry and metal. A cap is cheap compared with the water damage it prevents, and it pairs well with clean [gutter guards](/best-gutter-guards/) on the roof below to keep debris and runoff under control.

sections.h: What Sealant Works on Chimney Flashing?

blocks.p: For small gaps where counterflashing meets the brick, use a high-quality polyurethane or a sealant the label rates for metal-to-masonry flashing joints. For flashing that is rusted, holed, missing pieces or pulled out of the mortar, sealant is a stopgap; the fix is new flashing.

On a properly built chimney, counterflashing is let into the mortar joints: a slot is cut into a joint, the bent top edge of the flashing is set into it, and the slot is sealed. When that sealant dries and cracks, water runs behind the flashing. Clean out the old material, make sure the flashing is seated, and reseal the slot with a flexible sealant rated for masonry and metal that can handle the chimney's temperature swings. Avoid silicone where paint or another sealant may need to bond later.

Flashing and seal tapes can cover a small gap or hold a leak until a roofer arrives, and owner reviews are mixed on how long they last on a chimney exposed to sun and freeze-thaw. Treat them as a temporary patch. They do not replace counterflashing set into the mortar.

Failed flashing usually means removing shingles around the chimney, installing new step flashing and counterflashing cut into the mortar joints, and reshingling. That is roofing work. Sealant or tar smeared over badly failed flashing tends to crack and hold water within a season.

For joint sealant choices beyond flashing, including metal and masonry joints, the [best exterior caulk](/best-exterior-caulk/) guide compares polymer, polyurethane and tripolymer sealants. The same preparation rules from [caulking exterior windows](/how-to-caulk-exterior-windows/) apply: remove the old bead, clean to sound material, and lay sealant in a dry joint.

sections.h: How Do You Clean and Seal the Outside of a Chimney?

blocks.p: Work on a cold, dry chimney in mild weather. The fireplace and any appliance venting through the chimney should be off and cool for at least a day, the brick should have had no rain for 24 hours or more, and the forecast should be clear through the label's cure window. Roughly 40 to 90 degrees Fahrenheit suits most repellents.

ol: **Clean the brick.** Use a masonry cleaner and a stiff brush to remove dirt, moss and staining. Avoid high-pressure washing, which erodes mortar.
**Repair first.** Replace spalled bricks, repoint eroded joints and let new mortar cure for the time its maker lists. Fix the crown and flashing in the same project.
**Protect the surroundings.** Cover roofing, windows and siding below with plastic sheeting or drop cloths.
**Spray from the top down.** With a low-pressure pump sprayer, flood the brick so the repellent runs a few inches below the spray line. Apply a second coat wet on wet if the label calls for it.
**Cover all four sides.** Including the one facing away from the ladder.
**Let it cure.** Keep it dry for the label's cure time. Water should bead on the brick within a few days.
**Check after the first heavy rain.** If the leak continues, revisit the crown and flashing.

blocks.p: Roof work is the dangerous part. Use a ladder rated for your weight plus tools, tie it off and set it at a safe angle. On steep or high roofs, use a fall-arrest harness and roof anchor, or hire the job out. Never spray repellent into the flue or onto a warm chimney, and keep solvent products away from flames and pilot lights.

Many can, on a low-pitched roof that is easy to reach with a secured ladder. Cleaning, spraying and brushing on a crown coating are straightforward. Steep roofs, tall multi-story chimneys, flashing replacement and crown rebuilds are better left to a chimney or roofing professional.

sections.h: How Much Does It Cost to Waterproof a Chimney?

blocks.p: A do-it-yourself repellent job is the cheapest part of chimney maintenance. A typical single-flue chimney has roughly 100 to 200 square feet of brick above the roofline, which a gallon or two of repellent covers depending on how porous the brick is. Add a pump sprayer and plastic sheeting, and the materials for the brick are modest.

Chimney companies commonly quote professional waterproofing, often bundled with an inspection and a crown coating, from a few hundred dollars to around $1,000. Crown rebuilds, flashing replacement and repointing add substantially, and major masonry repair on a badly deteriorated chimney can reach several thousand dollars. Ask for a line-item quote so you can see what is repellent and what is repair.

blocks.h3: What it costs to skip it

blocks.p: Water damage to the framing, drywall and insulation around a chimney is expensive to repair, and chimneys that spall badly may need partial rebuilding above the roof. An annual inspection and a repellent every several years cost far less.

Quality penetrating repellents are commonly rated by their makers for 5 to 10 years or more, depending on exposure and brick porosity. South- and west-facing sides and exposed chimneys wear faster. Every year or two, spray a test area with a hose: when the brick darkens and stays dark instead of beading, it is time to reapply. Penetrating repellents do not need stripping first; clean the brick and spray a fresh coat. Check crown coatings each year as well, and touch up thin spots before winter.

sections.h: What Should You Never Seal: the Flue, Liner and Firebox?

blocks.p: Every product in this guide is for the outside of the chimney. None is rated for the inside of a flue, the firebox or the smoke chamber, which see high heat, corrosive combustion byproducts and creosote. Spraying a repellent or coating there can leave a flammable residue or give off fumes the next time the fireplace is lit.

The joint where a flue liner exits the crown should have a bond break or a flexible, heat-rated sealant specified by the liner or cap maker, so the liner can expand without cracking the crown. Do not fill it with rigid mortar or a standard exterior caulk.

Joints on metal chimney pipe and stove pipe use high-temperature sealants or cements rated for that use, and many factory-built chimney systems rely on their own locking joints rather than sealant at all. Follow the chimney system maker's instructions; an ordinary masonry sealer is the wrong product.

Liners that are cracked, missing tiles or have open joints need repair methods designed for them, such as a stainless steel relining kit or a professionally installed heat-rated resurfacing system. A damaged liner can let heat reach combustible framing and let carbon monoxide into the house. Firebox brick with failed joints is repaired with refractory mortar rated for fireplace temperatures, not masonry sealer or standard mortar.

If you notice smoke in the room, a strong creosote smell or soot staining on the outside of the chimney, stop using the fireplace and have it inspected before any waterproofing. A water problem can wait a week; a compromised flue cannot.

mistakes: Putting paint, tar or a gloss sealer on chimney brick

Film-forming coatings trap moisture inside the masonry, where it freezes and breaks off the brick face. Roofing tar on brick or crowns cracks and holds water. Use only repellents the label calls vapor permeable on the brick, and keep coatings for the crown, using products made for that surface.
Sealing the brick when the flashing is the leak

Many leaks blamed on brick come from failed counterflashing or a cracked crown. Sealing the brick leaves those paths wide open and the stain keeps spreading. Hose-test the chimney one section at a time to find the entry point, then fix the crown and flashing along with treating the brick.
Spraying a warm or recently used chimney

Repellent on warm masonry can flash off before it soaks in, and solvent products near heat are a fire risk. Leave the fireplace and anything that vents through the chimney off and cold for at least a day, and do the job on a mild, dry morning.
Skipping repairs to spalled brick and mortar

Sealer cannot rebuild a broken brick face or fill an eroded joint, and those spots let water deep into the chimney. Replace damaged brick, repoint the joints, let the mortar cure for the time its maker lists, then apply repellent so it protects sound masonry.

Most chimney work happens high up on a slope. Unsecured ladders, wet shingles and working alone cause serious falls. Tie off the ladder, wear a harness on steep pitches and keep a helper on the ground. If the roof is high or steep, hire a chimney professional.
bottomLine: ChimneySaver Water Repellent is the best chimney sealer for most homes, with Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 the pick for dense brick or for treating the chimney and the house walls together, and DRYLOK Clear Masonry Water Repellent the easy-to-find budget option. Pair any of them with ChimneyRX or CrownSeal on a sound crown, reseal or replace failing flashing, and fit a cap. Above all, find the leak before you buy: crowns, flashing and caps let in more water than brick does, and an annual inspection catches all of them early.

faqs.q: What type of breathable sealant should I use for spalling chimney brick?
faqs.a: Use a penetrating siloxane or silane-siloxane water repellent that the label calls vapor permeable, such as ChimneySaver Water Repellent or Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500. Repair first: replace spalled bricks, repoint eroded mortar and let it cure. Avoid paint, gloss sealers and tar, which trap moisture in the brick and make spalling worse.

faqs.q: What is the best chimney sealer?
faqs.a: ChimneySaver Water Repellent is the best chimney sealer for most brick chimneys because it is made for chimney masonry and keeps high vapor permeability. Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 suits dense brick, DRYLOK Clear Masonry Water Repellent is the budget pick, and ChimneyRX or ChimneySaver CrownSeal handle hairline cracks in the crown.

faqs.q: What can be put on chimney brick to stop leakage?
faqs.a: A breathable penetrating water repellent stops rain soaking through the brick and mortar. It will not stop leaks from a cracked crown, failed flashing or a missing cap, which are more common sources. Hose-test the chimney one area at a time to find the entry point, fix that part, then treat the brick so it stays dry.

faqs.q: What is the best sealer for a chimney crown?
faqs.a: An elastomeric crown coating such as ChimneyRX Brushable Crown Repair or ChimneySaver CrownSeal is best for a sound crown with hairline cracks. It bridges small cracks and flexes with temperature changes. A crown that is crumbling, broken or built without an overhang needs to be rebuilt in concrete, because a coating will not hold on failing material.

faqs.q: Will sealing the brick stop my chimney leak?
faqs.a: Only if the brick is where the water gets in. Many chimney leaks come from cracked crowns, failed flashing or a missing cap. A hose test with a helper watching inside shows which part leaks. Treating the brick is still worth doing to protect the masonry, but pair it with repairs to whichever part is actually leaking.

faqs.q: How long does chimney water repellent last?
faqs.a: Quality penetrating repellents are commonly rated by their makers for 5 to 10 years or more, depending on exposure and brick porosity. South- and west-facing sides wear faster. Spray a test patch with a hose every year or two; when the brick darkens and stays dark instead of beading water, clean it and reapply.

faqs.q: Will a chimney sealer make the brick look wet or shiny?
faqs.a: No, a penetrating repellent is designed to dry clear with no sheen or color change. The brick can look darker for a few hours while it is wet with product, then returns to normal. Crown coatings are visible but sit on top of the chimney where few people see them. Avoid gloss sealers, which change the look and trap moisture.
